title: Design and implement a prefix tree (Trie) supporting three operations: insert a word, search whether an exact word exists, and check whether any stored word starts with a given prefix.

s1_definition.profdef: A Trie is a tree where each edge represents one character, so every path from the root spells a prefix, and a boolean end-of-word flag on a node marks that the prefix spelled so far is a complete stored word. Insert, exact search, and prefix search all walk the tree one character at a time in time proportional to the length of the key, independent of how many words are stored.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the bank's directory of IFSC branch codes, where each code is typed digit by digit at the counter. The Trie is like a nested set of pigeonholes: the first character picks the first drawer, the next character picks a drawer inside it, and so on. A little flag inside a drawer says "a full valid code ends here." Searching a code or checking whether any code begins with a few typed characters just means following the drawers.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Trie stores words character by character along tree edges, with an end-of-word flag per node, giving insert, search, and prefix checks in time equal to the key length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Trie is a tree where each edge represents one character, so every path from the root spells a prefix, and a boolean end-of-word flag on a node marks that the prefix spelled so far is a complete stored word. Insert, exact search, and prefix search all walk the tree one character at a time in time proportional to the length of the key, independent of how many words are stored.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the bank's directory of IFSC branch codes, where each code is typed digit by digit at the counter. The Trie is like a nested set of pigeonholes: the first character picks the first drawer, the next character picks a drawer inside it, and so on. A little flag inside a drawer says "a full valid code ends here." Searching a code or checking whether any code begins with a few typed characters just means following the drawers.

**One line to remember:** A Trie stores words character by character along tree edges, with an end-of-word flag per node, giving insert, search, and prefix checks in time equal to the key length.

sections.s2_technical:
Each Trie node holds a map or fixed array of child links keyed by character, plus a boolean marking whether a word ends at that node. The root represents the empty prefix. For example: `class TrieNode { Map<Character,TrieNode> children = new HashMap<>(); boolean isWord; }`.

Insert walks the word character by character from the root, creating a child node whenever the path does not yet exist, then marks the final node as a word end. For example: `node = node.children.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new TrieNode());`.

Exact search walks the same path and, if it never falls off the tree, returns whether the final node has its end-of-word flag set. For example: `return node != null && node.isWord;`. The prefix check is identical except it returns true as long as the path exists, ignoring the end-of-word flag, because we only care that some word continues past the prefix.

The key property is that all three operations cost time proportional to the length of the key, not the number of stored keys, because each step follows exactly one child link. Space is proportional to the total number of characters across all inserted words in the worst case. A senior nuance is the choice between a HashMap of children (flexible alphabet, slightly more memory and pointer chasing) versus a fixed array of size twenty-six for lowercase letters (faster and cache-friendlier but wasteful for sparse alphabets).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the online portal offers type-ahead suggestions for IFSC branch codes as the customer types. The system must confirm whether a typed code is a complete valid code and whether any valid code begins with the characters typed so far. This is exactly how a Trie works — it answers exact-match and prefix queries in time proportional to the typed length.

Problem 2 — The directory holds hundreds of thousands of codes, so a solution whose cost grows with the number of stored codes per keystroke would be too slow. This is exactly why a Trie is used, since each keystroke costs only one step down the tree.

The mini-project builds a `BranchCodeTrie` with insert, search, and startsWith, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo that loads a few branch codes and answers queries.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three branch codes inserted, followed by four queries.

Step 1: Inserting NBIN0001234 walks from the root creating one child per character, N then B then I and so on, and marks the final node after the last 4 as an end-of-word.

Step 2: Inserting NBIN0005678 reuses the shared prefix NBIN000 nodes already created, and only branches at the differing character, creating new nodes from there to the end.

Step 3: The exact search for NBIN0001234 follows the existing path to the final node and finds its end-of-word flag set, returning true.

Step 4: The exact search for NBIN0001 follows a valid path but the node it lands on has no end-of-word flag, because no full code ends there, so it returns false.

Step 5: The prefix check for NBIN000 follows the shared path and succeeds because the node exists, returning true regardless of end-of-word.

Step 6: The prefix check for HDFC fails at the very first character because the root has no H child, returning false immediately.

```text
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Branch Code Type-Ahead (Trie)
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Inserted branch code: NBIN0001234
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Inserted branch code: NBIN0005678
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Inserted branch code: NBIN0009999
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Exact search 'NBIN0001234' -> true
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Exact search 'NBIN0001' -> false
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Prefix 'NBIN000' -> true
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Prefix 'HDFC' -> false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  root
   └─N─B─I─N─0─0─0─┬─1─2─3─4●   (NBIN0001234, ●=isWord)
                   ├─5─6─7─8●   (NBIN0005678)
                   └─9─9─9─9●   (NBIN0009999)

  search("NBIN0001234") → reaches ● → true
  search("NBIN0001")    → node exists but no ● → false
  startsWith("NBIN000") → node exists → true
  startsWith("HDFC")    → no 'H' child at root → false
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Trie (insert/search/startsWith) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Tree of nodes keyed by character (prefix sharing)        │
  │  computeIfAbsent creates path lazily on insert            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: TrieNode holds links+flag; Trie owns operations       │
  │  O: alphabet swap (HashMap ↔ array[26]) without API change│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   BranchCodeTrie                      │
  │  + insert(code): void                 │ O(len)
  │  + search(code): boolean              │ O(len), checks isWord
  │  + startsWith(prefix): boolean        │ O(len), path-only
  │  - walk(s): TrieNode                  │ shared traversal
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract: search true iff full word stored; startsWith true iff path exists.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Trie is a prefix tree where each edge carries one character, so every path from the root spells a prefix, and a boolean end-of-word flag on a node tells me that the prefix spelled up to that node is a complete stored word. The power of this structure is that insert, exact search, and prefix search all cost time proportional only to the length of the key, never to the number of keys stored, because each step follows exactly one child link.

Insert walks the word from the root, using computeIfAbsent to create a child node whenever the path does not yet exist, and marks the last node as a word end. Exact search walks the same path and returns true only if it reaches the end without falling off the tree and the final node has its end-of-word flag set. The prefix check is the same walk but returns true as soon as the path exists, ignoring the flag, because for a prefix I only care that some word continues beyond it.

The subtle point interviewers listen for is the difference between search and startsWith: both traverse identically, but search additionally requires the end-of-word flag, while startsWith does not. I also mention the design trade-off between a HashMap of children, which handles any alphabet flexibly, and a fixed array of twenty-six for lowercase letters, which is faster and more cache-friendly but wasteful on sparse alphabets.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used a Trie to power type-ahead for IFSC branch codes on the portal. Each keystroke calls startsWith to decide whether to keep offering suggestions and search to tell whether the typed string is already a complete valid code. Because the directory holds hundreds of thousands of codes, a per-keystroke cost that grew with the directory size would have been unacceptable, and the Trie kept every keystroke proportional to just the few characters typed.
